questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Expression for the Upper Bound in Terms of Maximum Values
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/f77ec60f3208cd221570e30ed8f4c1684607dc54567435071dd34ccf76ea5227.png)

Consider the partition of the rectangular region $R$ shown above and the positive function $f(x,y)$ defined on $R.$ Which of the following gives an expression for the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition.

*Hint: ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}$*
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the upper Riemann sum $U$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $2$ rectangular solids, one for each ${R}_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion ${R}_{ij}$ is given by

$$
{M}_{ij}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{ij}).
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
U={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12}).
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{11})=1
$$

and

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{12})=3.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}U & ={M}_{11}+3\cdot {M}_{12} \\  & ={M}_{11}+3{M}_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Upper Riemann Sum in the Case of a Strictly Decreasing Function
questions.problem:
Let $R=[1,3]\times [2,4]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=30-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={1,2,3},\,{P}_{2}={2,3,4},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the upper Riemann sum $U(f,P).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/b7581f31a2031181aeb31bbdf8a3da6beff69b50ee41d5d73babbe198997fe15.png)

The upper sum $U(f,P)$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{M}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22}),
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=1$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $U(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
U(f,P)={M}_{11}+{M}_{21}+{M}_{12}+{M}_{22}.
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=30-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=30-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/dfed66710976869aa4507aea2e171c09ac248d4b8b4ca083972dbd10952af6b7.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$in each subregion is attained when we have the *smallest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom left corner* of each subregion.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/a6366799e116eb35e8d3cb5401f0abc161ad183cd8f634bdaf2ce387f64d6c5c.png)

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{11} & =f(1,2)=25 \\ {M}_{21} & =f(2,2)=22 \\ {M}_{12} & =f(1,3)=20 \\ {M}_{22} & =f(2,3)=17\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =25+22+20+17 \\  & =84.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={-2,0,2},\,{P}_{2}={-2,0,2},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the upper Riemann sum $U(f,P).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/6a44295e07e8d14dfae78403d4629bde77c522136d5ffec16ace6416db72303e.png)

The upper sum $U(f,P)$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{M}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22}),
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=4$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $U(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =4\cdot {M}_{11}+4\cdot {M}_{21}+4\cdot {M}_{12}+4\cdot {M}_{22} \\  & =4({M}_{11}+{M}_{21}+{M}_{12}+{M}_{22}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=2x+y+10$ increases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=2x+y+10$ increases as $y$ increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/bdb4b6095c1b449d8e048f85a0d4d289758597af520ed61f545dbe280560ca15.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/ca1c7e423afd88b0f1b18570bad73897092167ad338dcdbe275aaf451a08b3cb.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{11} & =f(0,0)=10 \\ {M}_{21} & =f(2,0)=14 \\ {M}_{12} & =f(0,2)=12 \\ {M}_{22} & =f(2,2)=16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =4(10+14+12+16) \\  & =208.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Expression for the Upper Bound in Terms of Maximum Values
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072318/assets/33269c79413f4435d074d90cd727f2a53e7b9831300bfcaf0b5a7122df764080.png)

Consider the partition of the rectangular region $R$ shown above and the positive function $f(x,y)$ defined on $R.$ Find an expression for the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition.

*Hint: $M_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion $R_{ij}$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the upper Riemann sum $U$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $2$ rectangular solids, one for each $R_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion $R_{ij}$ is given by

$$
M_{ij}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{ij}).
$$

where $M_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion $R_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
U = M_{11}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{11}) + M_{21}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{21}).
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\textrm{Area}(R_{11}) = 8
$$

and

$$
\textrm{Area}(R_{21}) = 4.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =8\cdot {M}_{11}+4\cdot {M}_{21} \\  & =8{M}_{11}+4{M}_{21}.\end{aligned}
$$
